title: API Boundaries and Separation of Concerns
learningObjectives: Explain the key boundary or design principle in this topic.
Identify a clear responsibility and interface in a code example.
Describe how a caller uses a component without depending on its internals.
Recognize duplication or cohesion problems and their trade-offs.
Apply the principle to a small program design.

understand.concept: An API boundary is the defined way one component communicates with another. Separation of concerns means each part of a program handles a distinct responsibility, such as data access, calculations, user interaction, or presentation. A boundary hides internal details and exposes only the capability callers need. These ideas can apply to functions, modules, services, or entire applications.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear boundaries reduce the number of details a component must know about, making it easier to change or test one part without rewriting everything else. Boundaries that are too rigid or too numerous can also add complexity.
understand.analogy: A restaurant customer orders from a menu rather than entering the kitchen and controlling every cooking step. The menu is the public boundary; the analogy does not capture all technical constraints, error handling, or data contracts.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy provides a starting point but cannot replace technical contracts, runtime behavior, or project-specific design decisions.

explain.narrative: Define the responsibility of each component and the data or operations it exposes. Keep callers dependent on the public contract rather than internal implementation. Separate presentation, business rules, and storage when that separation makes change or testing easier.

examples.title: Caller uses a small interface
examples.explanation: The caller supplies data and receives a result without knowing how summation is implemented.

examples.title: Separate formatting from calculation
examples.explanation: Calculation and display formatting have distinct responsibilities.

examples.title: Hide internal detail behind a function
examples.explanation: Callers use the named rule rather than repeating the internal comparison.

examples.title: Stable boundary
examples.explanation: A caller depends on the function's input/output contract; implementation can be revised without changing the call shape.

examples.title: Avoid leaking internal state
examples.explanation: A function can expose a needed value while keeping the caller focused on the interface.

commonMistakes: Combining unrelated responsibilities in one function.
Extracting abstractions that are harder to understand than the original code.
Assuming all similar-looking code has identical rules.
Changing a public contract without updating callers or tests.

guidedTask.title: Guided practice: API Boundaries and Separation of Concerns
guidedTask.instructions: Review a small program, identify its responsibilities, and improve the boundary or cohesion without changing intended behavior.
steps: Identify the function or component that mixes or exposes too much.
Propose a clear interface and focused responsibility.
Make a small change and test two cases.
Explain why the new boundary is or is not an improvement.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Start with a small function; separate responsibilities if doing so improves clarity.

independentTask.title: Independent practice: maintainable component design
independentTask.instructions: Design or refactor a small workflow using focused functions and clear boundaries.
requirements: Explain one trade-off or limitation of the design.

hints: Keep public interfaces small and clear.
Separate calculation from effects when helpful.
Review whether your abstraction makes the code simpler.

questions.prompt: What does a clear component boundary help achieve?
options: Limit callers to a defined interface instead of internal details
Require every caller to know implementation internals
Eliminate the need for error handling
questions.answer: Limit callers to a defined interface instead of internal details
questions.explanation: Boundaries make dependencies clearer and can allow internal changes without changing callers.

questions.prompt: What is a sign of a cohesive function?
options: Its statements support one focused responsibility
It performs unrelated tasks with no clear purpose
Its name does not describe its work
questions.answer: Its statements support one focused responsibility
questions.explanation: Cohesion means related work belongs together within a focused unit.

questions.prompt: When is extracting repeated logic most useful?
options: When the repeated behavior is stable and one shared rule improves consistency
Whenever two lines have any words in common
When abstraction is required regardless of clarity
questions.answer: When the repeated behavior is stable and one shared rule improves consistency
questions.explanation: Reuse should reduce duplication and improve maintainability without obscuring intent.

questions.prompt: Why should similar code sometimes remain separate?
options: It may represent different policies or requirements
questions.answer: It may represent different policies or requirements
questions.explanation: Blindly combining distinct rules can hide differences and create incorrect behavior.

questions.prompt: Which review criterion is most useful for a refactor?
options: The code remains correct and becomes clearer or easier to change
All details are moved behind hidden names
questions.answer: The code remains correct and becomes clearer or easier to change
questions.explanation: A refactor should preserve behavior while improving structure, clarity, or maintainability.
